start: The current of a running stream flows on unceasingly
end: Such are mankind and their habitations.
context: The famous opening of Hōjōki ('An Account of My Ten-Foot Hut', 1212), written by a poet who withdrew to a tiny mountain hut after years of fire, famine and earthquake.
prompt: What in your life is the same river, but different water?

source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. I
start: Those who cannot feel the littleness of great things in themselves
end: greatness of little things in others.
context: Okakura aims this at Western readers who saw the tea ceremony as a quaint oddity. People too sure of their own importance miss the value of small things in others. Humility is what lets us see it.
prompt: What small thing in someone else have you overlooked?

start: The perfect circle of the full moon lasts only for a very short time
context: Kenkō was a 14th-century poet and monk whose short essays on beauty and impermanence remain beloved in Japan. Change, he notes, is often too slow to see.
prompt: What is quietly changing in your life, too slowly to notice?

source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. I
start: Teaism is a cult founded on the adoration of the beautiful
end: this impossible thing we know as life.
context: Okakura's definition of the tea ceremony's spirit: finding beauty in ordinary life, and honouring what is imperfect.
prompt: Where could you find beauty in the ordinary today?

start: A certain man who was learning archery
end: this particular shaft at any cost.
context: A teacher tells his student to carry only one arrow, because a second one makes the first careless. Kenkō applies it to every moment of life.
prompt: What 'second arrow' is making you careless with the first?

source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. I
start: Let us dream of evanescence
context: The closing line of Okakura's first chapter: an invitation to slow down and savour what passes.
prompt: What passing thing could you linger over today?

parts: Is it only when the flowers are in full bloom
The twigs which bear no blossoms as yet
context: Kenkō's most famous essay. Beauty isn't only in the peak moment, but in anticipation, in absence, and in what has already passed.
prompt: What 'not yet' or 'no longer' could you admire today?

source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. III
start: The art of life lies in a constant readjustment to our surroundings.
context: Okakura draws on Taoism: there is no fixed recipe for living well, only continual, graceful adjustment.
prompt: What change around you are you resisting instead of adjusting to?

start: The dew upon Adashi Moor never fades away
context: Adashi Moor and Toribe Moor were burial grounds near Kyoto. If life never ended, Kenkō says, we would lose our tenderness. Not knowing how long we have is a gift.
prompt: How does knowing life is uncertain make it more precious to you?

source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. II
start: Perhaps we reveal ourselves too much in small things
end: so little of the great to conceal.
context: A wry line. Our small, unconscious habits give us away, Okakura says, perhaps because we have less grandeur to hide than we like to think.
prompt: What do your small daily habits say about you?

start: Nobody ever grudges a moment of time
end: life's end comes all too suddenly.
context: Like a merchant careful with each coin, Kenkō asks us to value each moment, since moments are what a life is made of.
prompt: Which moments are you spending without noticing?

source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. III
parts: The usefulness of a water pitcher dwelt in the emptiness
One who could make of himself a vacuum into which others might freely enter
context: Okakura echoes Laozi: emptiness is what makes things useful, and a person who leaves room for others can meet any situation.
prompt: How could you leave more room for others to enter?

start: Nothing is more refreshing than to make friends with those who are no longer
context: Kenkō's picture of reading: a quiet evening spent in conversation with the long dead.
prompt: Which writer from the past would you like to spend an evening with?

source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. IV
start: True beauty could be discovered only by one who mentally completed the incomplete.
context: In the tea room, things are left deliberately unfinished so that each guest completes them in their own imagination.
prompt: What unfinished thing could you appreciate as it is?

start: the order of the four seasons is fixed, while none know the time of death
context: Seasons arrive in order; death doesn't announce itself. Kenkō's image: the tide comes in while the beach still looks dry.
prompt: What would you stop postponing if you felt time pressing from behind?

source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. III
start: In leaving something unsaid the beholder is given a chance to complete the idea
context: Great art suggests rather than spells everything out, and that space is where we enter it.
prompt: What could you leave unsaid today, and let someone else complete?

start: He who afflicts his whole life by spending it in the pursuit of riches and fame
context: Kenkō's verdict on a life spent chasing wealth and reputation with no time left for stillness.
prompt: Is there enough leisure for quiet in your life?

start: It is barely ten feet square, and only seven feet high.
context: Chōmei's last home was a hut small enough to take apart and move on two carts. Owning little, he could not lose much.
prompt: What could you live without, and how would that lighten you?

source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. V
start: Nothing is more hallowing than the union of kindred spirits in art.
context: Okakura describes the moment when a work of art and its viewer truly meet, beyond words.
prompt: When did a piece of art last leave you without words?

start: How can a man ever find it wearisome to live at leisure?
context: Kenkō defends solitude: away from the noise of the world, we stop being blown about by everyone else's moods.
prompt: When did you last enjoy being alone?

source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. VII
start: He only who has lived with the beautiful can die beautifully.
context: Okakura writes of the great tea masters, who met even their deaths with the grace they had practised all their lives.
prompt: What beauty are you living with every day?

start: He who mixes with the experts while he is himself still stiff and imperfect
end: not lag far behind the others.
context: Waiting until we're good before practising in public means never getting good. Kenkō recommends being a beginner openly.
prompt: What are you avoiding because you're not good at it yet?

source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. IV
start: Young fool," chided the tea-master
context: The tea master Rikyū's lesson to a son who had swept the garden perfectly clean: real beauty needs a touch of the natural.
prompt: Where could you allow a few leaves to fall?

start: You may propose to do a certain thing to-day
end: only the unlooked for that actually happens.
context: Kenkō on plans: the day rarely goes as expected, and neither do years. Better to hold plans lightly.
prompt: What unexpected thing happened today, and what did it bring?

source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. IV
start: One cannot listen to different pieces of music at the same time
context: The tea room displays one beautiful object at a time. Okakura's point applies to attention in general.
prompt: What one thing deserves your full attention today?

start: Many are the things on which we should place no reliance
context: Kenkō lists the things we lean on (power, wealth, cleverness) and reminds us how quickly each can fail.
prompt: What are you relying on that could change in an instant?

start: When I first took up my abode in this place, I thought it was only for a little while.
end: moss has gathered on the earthen floor.
context: Chōmei meant his hut to be temporary. Five years later, moss covers the floor. Life settles in while we're still telling ourselves it's for a little while.
prompt: What 'temporary' arrangement in your life has quietly become permanent?

start: Generally speaking, uniformity in anything at all is bad
context: Kenkō praises frayed silk covers and mismatched books. Perfection, he suggests, leaves nothing to grow into.
prompt: Where could a little imperfection make something better?

source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. I
start: It is hygiene, for it enforces cleanliness
context: Okakura describes the tea ceremony as a whole way of life: cleanliness, simplicity, and a sense of our place in things.
prompt: Where could you choose the simple over the complex and costly?

start: The moon when full begins to wane
context: Kenkō on the danger of reaching the top: every peak is also the beginning of a descent.
prompt: Where could you be content with less than the very top?

start: When on a calm night the moon shines in at my window
context: Alone in his hut, Chōmei finds company in the moon and in the memory of those who lived before him.
prompt: Who from the past do you feel close to on a quiet night?

source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. IV
start: The tea-room is unimpressive in appearance.
context: The tea room is deliberately tiny and plain, built to suggest 'refined poverty', and every humble detail is carefully chosen.
prompt: Where could plainness be a kind of refinement in your life?

start: Nothing is harder to forsake than the customs and conventionalities of life
context: Kenkō observes how hard it is to step away from social obligations, even when we know they keep us from what matters.
prompt: Which convention are you keeping only out of habit?
